chapter.title: What an agent is, and what it is not

cards.body:
A chat window waits for you to type. An agent doesn't wait. Think of it as a person you pay to read the same 5 newspapers every morning, cut out only the stories about your rivals, and leave a short note on your desk.

**Nobody has to ask it each day, and in this course that's what we call an agent.**
cards.simpler: A chat window waits for you to type. An agent doesn't wait. Picture a person you pay to read the same 5 newspapers every morning. They cut out only the stories about your rivals and leave a short note on your desk. **Nobody has to ask it each day, and in this course that's what we call an agent.**

cards.prompt: Every Monday, Priya opens ChatGPT, pastes in a rival's pricing page and asks, "What changed?" She has done this for 9 weeks straight. Is that an agent?

options.text: Yes, because an AI model reads the page
No, because Priya has to start it every time
Yes, because it happens every single week

whyNot.a: That's the reader, not the whole service. A model reading text is one part, but nothing happens until Priya shows up.
whyNot.c: That's Priya's habit, not the program's. The weekly rhythm lives in her calendar, not in the tool.

cards.reteach: An agent starts itself. If a person has to press go each time, it's a tool, not an agent. The clipping service turns up at 7am whether you remember it or not.

cards.title: The first two boxes
cards.body:
In this course, an agent is a *program* (a set of steps a computer follows) that runs on its own and calls an AI model to read and write text. It has 4 parts. Here are the first 2.

The *trigger* is the alarm clock. It says when to start, say every day at 7:00. **No trigger, no agent.** Without one, it's just a tool sitting on a shelf.

The *sources* are the newspapers: the exact web pages it reads. Not "the internet". It's a short list of addresses, like a rival's pricing page, written down once and read every time.
cards.simpler: In this course, an agent is a program, a list of steps a computer follows, that runs by itself and asks an AI model to read and write text. It has 4 parts. First is the trigger, an alarm clock that says when to start, like 7:00 each day. **No trigger, no agent.** Second are the sources, the newspapers. These are a short list of exact web pages, like a rival's pricing page, read every time. Not the whole internet.

cards.title: 7:00 at Sam's desk
cards.body: Sam sells a $12-a-month booking app for hair salons. At 7:00 the trigger fires, and the agent opens 4 pages: two rivals' pricing pages, one changelog (a list of product updates) and one careers page. The model reads them and spots one thing: a rival's basic plan went from $10 to $14. At 7:02, Sam's note says exactly that, with the link. **Sam slept through all of it**, which is the whole point.
cards.simpler: Sam sells a $12-a-month booking app for hair salons. At 7:00 the trigger goes off. The agent opens 4 pages: two rivals' pricing pages, one changelog, which is a list of product updates, and one careers page. The model reads them and finds one thing. A rival's basic plan went from $10 to $14. At 7:02, Sam gets a note saying just that, with the link. **Sam slept through all of it**, and that is the whole point.

cards.prompt: Sam now wants the agent to read a rival's blog too. Where does that change go?

options.text: In the trigger, because it decides when the agent starts
In the sources, because it decides what the agent reads
Nowhere: Sam can just ask the model to "check the blog too" each morning

whyNot.a: That's the alarm clock, not the newspapers. The trigger sets when, not what.
whyNot.c: That's a person pressing go, not an agent. Asking every morning puts Sam back in charge of starting it.

cards.reteach: Each box answers one question. The trigger answers "when?" and the sources answer "what to read?" Adding a page is like adding a newspaper to the pile, so it goes in sources.

cards.title: The other two boxes
cards.body:
The *model* is the reader: an AI like Claude or ChatGPT that turns a page of text into a sentence worth reading. You'd think it's the clever part that runs the show. It isn't. **The model only reads what the other boxes hand it**, and it forgets everything once the job is done.

The *output* is the note on your desk: an email, a chat message or a file. If it lands in a folder you never open, the whole service worked for nobody.

So it goes alarm clock, newspapers, reader, note. Four boxes, one arrow running through them.
cards.simpler: The model is the reader. It's an AI like Claude or ChatGPT that turns a page of text into one useful sentence. It may seem like the boss, but it isn't. **The model only reads what the other boxes hand it**, and it forgets everything after. The output is the note on your desk, like an email, a chat message or a file. If no one opens it, the work was wasted. So: alarm clock, newspapers, reader, note.

cards.body: Jordan spends a weekend writing the perfect instructions for the model, then runs it by hand from their laptop every Friday. That's a brilliant reader with no alarm clock. To spot it, ask yourself: **if I went on holiday for a week, would anything still arrive?** If the answer is no, it's a tool, not an agent.
cards.simpler: Jordan spends a weekend writing perfect instructions for the model. Then Jordan runs it by hand from a laptop every Friday. That's a great reader with no alarm clock. Here's a quick test. Ask yourself: **if I went on holiday for a week, would anything still arrive?** If not, it's a tool, something you have to start yourself, not an agent.

cards.prompt: Sam's 7:02 note stopped arriving on Tuesday. When Sam runs the agent by hand, the note shows up perfectly. Which box broke?

whyNot.a: That's the newspapers, not the alarm clock. The hand run read every page fine.
whyNot.c: That's the note, not the alarm clock. The hand run delivered it fine.

cards.reteach: When Sam ran it by hand, every box worked, but Sam's own finger stood in for the alarm clock. So the alarm clock is the box that broke. To test any box, ask what you had to do yourself.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: An agent is a program that wakes itself up, reads a fixed list of pages, asks an AI model what they say and leaves you a note. **Four boxes: trigger, sources, model, output**, and in this course the trigger is the one that makes it an agent.
cards.simpler: An agent is a program that wakes itself up, reads a fixed list of pages, asks an AI model what they say and leaves you a note. **Four boxes: trigger, sources, model, output.** Think alarm clock, newspapers, reader, note. In this course, the trigger is the one that makes it an agent.

cards.body:
Grab a scrap of paper. Draw 4 boxes in a row and label them alarm clock, newspapers, reader and note. Under "newspapers", write the web address of the one rival page you'd check first.

Under newspapers, write the web address of the one rival page you would check first. Tomorrow: why watching 5 pages beats watching 50.

dubious_claims: "ChatGPT has never once messaged you first": ChatGPT Tasks (2025) and ChatGPT Pulse (2025) send updates to users without being asked

"Nobody has to ask it each day, and that is what makes it an agent" / "the trigger is the one that makes it an agent": most definitions (for example Anthropic's 'Building effective agents') say an agent is an AI that decides its own steps and tool use, and they call a timed program that calls an AI model a workflow, not an agent
"it's a script, not an agent" (card 7) uses a different word from "helper" (card 2) and "tool" (card 3) for the same thing, so the 'what it is not' side has three names
repairedFrom.why: Card 1 is the hook and the definition the whole chapter rests on, and both are shaky: ChatGPT can now message you first (scheduled Tasks, Pulse), and saying the trigger alone makes something an agent goes against the usual meaning, where the AI decides its own steps.
repairedFrom.fix: Change the opener to "A chat window waits for you to type. An agent doesn't wait." and change the bold line to "Nobody has to ask it each day, and in this course that's what we call an agent." Also move "Tomorrow: why watching 5 pages beats watching 50" so it comes after the try card and is the chapter's last line.
